claims.text: In CrFeCoNiX HEAs, protective-scale retention above 900 °C is primarily governed by the balance between outward cation diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion.
Al in CrFeCoNiAl can form a protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature oxidation.
Al2O3 scales grow more slowly than chromium-oxide scales and are comparatively stable.
A modest or slow outward diffusivity of Al relative to inward oxygen diffusion enables a continuous, adherent alumina scale.
High-temperature oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi can produce an oxide layer dominated by alpha-Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
Protective alumina formation in AlCoCrFeNi can involve grain-boundary diffusion of Al.
Mn promotes faster cation diffusion than Al in the proposed CrFeCoNiX comparison.
Mn additions lead to volatile or non-coherent manganese oxides.
Fast Mn-related diffusion produces rapid oxide growth and discontinuous scales that crack or spall.
A mismatch between inward and outward diffusion produces stresses and voids that cause scale cracking or spallation.
Si-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys form less-protective silicate phases.
CrFeCoNiSi has oxide-scale stability intermediate between CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiMn.
Adding Al improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to adding Mn or Si.
Oxidation in these alloys can be diffusion controlled and exhibit parabolic kinetics.
Alloy microstructure, surface heterogeneity, and phase stability can influence oxide-scale structure.
The proposed mechanism applies to both single-phase and multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions.
The proposed ranking applies above 900 °C in both oxidative and corrosive atmospheres, including chloride-containing environments.
Testing Al-, Mn-, and Si-containing alloys made with identical processing at 950 °C for 50–100 hours provides a controlled comparison of X.
The mechanism would be falsified if Mn- or Si-containing alloys formed stable, coherent, slow-growing scales while the Al-containing alloy did not.

contradictions.description: The intervention and boundary require temperatures strictly above 900 °C, but the illustrative conditions include 900 °C.

The baseline is ambiguously defined as either CrFeCoNi without X or an Al-containing HEA, while the predicted outcome treats Al addition as the improvement being evaluated. Using an Al-containing alloy as the baseline makes that comparison non-unique.
